study.title: Climate benefit and ecological cost trade-offs for ocean iron fertilization

cover.headline: The ocean's most-pitched climate fix buys months, not decades, and **charges the food web for it.**

slides.title: Sixty years of fertilising ten ocean regions bought between 1.1 and 5.3 ppm of CO2.
slides.body:
Humans add roughly 2.5 ppm every year. So six decades of non-stop seeding buys back somewhere between five months and two years of emissions.

More than half the captured carbon leaked back out within decades of stopping.

stat.label: best case, after 60 years of seeding

slides.title: Iron seeding is the cheapest ocean climate fix on the table, and it cannot carry the load.
slides.body:
Every ton not removed here is a ton that has to come from cutting emissions instead. The paper calls it a trade-off, not a fix.

The bill is paid twice: less carbon banked, and a thinner food web.

slides.title: Iron is the missing nutrient across a third of the ocean. Add it, and plankton bloom.
slides.body:
Plankton pull carbon out of the air and sink when they die, carrying it to the deep sea. Starve them of iron and they never get going.

Add iron and you get a bloom. Nobody had modelled that ocean-wide.

caveats: This is a computer model, not an experiment. No iron was actually dumped in any ocean.
Equatorial seeding shrank zooplankton and widened low-oxygen dead zones. The food web pays.
Over half the captured carbon came back out. The ocean is a leaky bank, not a vault.

cta.headline: Send this to whoever calls ocean iron a climate fix
cta.sub: One real study, every weekday. The full paper is linked in bio.

caption: The ocean's most-pitched climate fix buys months of emissions, not decades, and the food web picks up the tab.
